lesson.title: Same Address, Nearest Answer: The Trick Behind Anycast
lesson.summary: Anycast assigns the identical IP address to multiple physically distributed servers, and ordinary internet routing automatically delivers each sender's packet to whichever instance is topologically closest, giving lower latency and built-in resilience without the sender doing anything special.
lesson.body:
Anycast looks, from a sender's point of view, exactly like unicast: a packet is addressed to a single IP address, and the sender neither knows nor cares that anything unusual is happening. The trick is on the receiving side. That same IP address is announced from multiple, often widely distributed, physical locations at once, and normal internet routing, specifically BGP, the protocol that exchanges reachability information between networks, treats each announcement as a legitimate path to that address. Because BGP naturally prefers shorter, cheaper paths, a router forwarding an anycast-addressed packet ends up sending it toward whichever announcing location is topologically nearest to it, without any special anycast-aware logic anywhere in the path.

The clearest large-scale example is the DNS root server system. The root servers are reachable through a small set of IP addresses, but each of those addresses is actually announced from dozens or even hundreds of physical server sites scattered across the globe, all answering as though they were the single canonical root server for that address. A resolver in Tokyo querying one of these addresses gets routed to a nearby instance in Asia, while a resolver in New York querying the identical address gets routed to a nearby instance in North America, purely because BGP routing sent each query toward its own closest announcing site. Google's public DNS service at 8.8.8.8 works the same way: it is one address on paper, but many machines in many places answer to it depending on where the query originates.

This is why anycast fits naturally alongside unicast, multicast, and broadcast as a network layer delivery mode built on IP addressing, even though it behaves so differently underneath. It gives three real benefits at once. Latency drops, since queries are automatically routed to a nearby instance rather than one fixed, possibly distant, server. Load naturally spreads across instances, since nearby senders are distributed among nearby sites. And resilience improves significantly, because if one anycast site goes down or is overwhelmed, say by a denial-of-service attack, BGP simply stops hearing that site's announcement and reroutes traffic to the next-nearest surviving instance, all without the sender changing anything or even noticing.

The cost is operational complexity: keeping many geographically separate instances synchronized, and correctly announcing the same prefix from multiple autonomous systems, requires careful coordination that a single unicast server never has to worry about. It also matters that BGP's routing decisions can change mid-conversation, which is fine for a single, quick DNS query over UDP but risky for a long-lived TCP connection, since a route change partway through could suddenly redirect later packets of that same connection to a different physical instance that knows nothing about it. That is why anycast is used most confidently for short, stateless, connectionless exchanges, and used only with careful additional engineering for anything longer-lived. For services where availability and low latency at global scale matter enormously, DNS infrastructure and content delivery networks being the leading examples, that complexity is a worthwhile trade.
